newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - Jan 20.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - Jan 20.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories Monday:
* The World Trade Organization ruled that Canada cannot ban Canadian editions of magazines from the United States through measures that hurt trade.
* U.S. Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary said the price of energy is artificially depressed in the United States.
* Japan has become one of the world's fastest growing markets for mobile telephones, gaining more than one million new subscribers each month.

* Malaysian Prime Minister visited California's Silicon Valley and met with executives from Microsoft Corp, Netscape Communications Corp, Oracle Corp, Sun Microsystems Inc and Hewlett-Packard to present his vision of a "multimedia supercorridor" in Malaysia.
* Los Angeles is at the beginning of a stage-building boom and rental costs for studio space are rising as the numbers of television networks, movies and music videos increase.
* Microsoft, Netscape, and Apple Computer Inc plan to make use of "push" technology that would make the delivery of information on the Internet more like its delivery on television.
* New York's WBIS station, owned by Dow Jones & Co Inc and by ITT Corp, the co-owner of Madison Square Garden, begins combining daytime business newscasts with sports news at night.
* William Barr, a former U.S. Attorney General under President George Bush, is leading a landmark case by representing GTE Corp in its challenge of the Telecommunications Act of 1996.

* Finland is becoming a model of an electronic future, with twice the proportion of Internet host computers than the United States and the number of people carrying mobile phones increasing by 27 percent a year.
* Twenty-six months after its debut, DreamWorks SKG, the entertainment company started by Jeffrey Katzenberg, Steven Spielberg and David Geffen, is still waiting to make its first big splash.

* The Pentagon has proposed lifting the last restrictions on its private stores, or P.X.'s, which protect small businesses around military bases, arguing that such stores have mostly succumbed to large retail chains.
* Supporters of communications technology include Congressional leaders from rural areas who believe technological advances will bring economic development to their districts.
